title: Redwood discovery - Archon Payments - latency & throughput
next_steps: Redwood to send hosted vs dedicated pricing sheet
SE to run 1-hour token/sec benchmark on Archon's sample workload and share results
Send SOC2 + security architecture doc and VPC deployment checklist
Schedule dedicated pilot kickoff in two weeks
action_items: Maya: Share pricing and contract template (2026-08-22)
Liam: Run throughput benchmark with 256-token prompts and streaming enabled, share logs (2026-08-24)
Sofia: Provide sample workload and p95 target profiles (2026-08-21)
Tom: Confirm network egress and VPC peering constraints, provide contact for infra integration (2026-08-25)
header:
Date: 2026-08-20
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO, Archon), Sofia Martinez (Head of ML, Archon), Tom Jensen (Infra Manager, Archon)
Meeting recorded: yes
Notes: discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency, streaming, and token/sec benchmarking.
summary: Customer (Archon Payments) evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment. Primary concerns: p95 latency under 100ms for short responses, concurrency ~300-500 concurrent requests during peak, streaming needed for progressive responses in payments UI, and realistic tokens/sec throughput for 256-512 token prompts. Discussed benchmarking approach, SOC2/KMS requirements, and VPC options. Agreed next steps: pricing, sample workload for benchmark, SE-run token/sec test, share security docs, schedule pilot kickoff.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the account lead on this. We also have Liam, our solutions engineer.
[00:00:10] Raj: Hi, Raj here. Thanks, Maya. Sofia and Tom are on as well.
[00:00:16] Sofia: Hey all.
[00:00:18] Tom: Hi.
[00:00:22] Maya: Cool, the plan for today is a quick intro, then go deep on your latency and throughput targets, streaming needs, and we'll talk deployment options — hosted, dedicated, private — and what the tradeoffs look like. Sound good?
[00:00:33] Raj: Yep, that works. We're specifically trying to understand if Redwood's Hosted API can hit our p95 SLAs for user-facing payments flows.
[00:00:40] Liam: Great, can you share your current targets? Like p95 numbers, concurrency, and typical prompt sizes?
[00:00:46] Sofia: Sure, at a high level our p95 target is sub-100ms for short completion responses — think auth decisions and fraud flags, mostly under 64 tokens. For larger items like account summary generation we can tolerate up to 400ms p95.
[00:01:02] Raj: Concurrency wise we need to be able to handle around 300 concurrent inference calls during peak, with burst capacity to ~500 for seasonal spikes.
[00:01:10] Tom: Also important we need streaming in the front-end for progressive disclosure — the UI expects token-level partial updates.
[00:01:18] Liam: That's helpful. Two quick clarifications: when you say sub-100ms p95, is that end-to-end from client to final token, including network and SDK overhead, or do you mean server-side generation time only?
[00:01:30] Sofia: Good point — we mean perceived latency in the app, so client->server->response basically end-to-end. But we can provide a breakdown; our app overhead is typically ~20-30ms.
[00:01:40] Maya: Okay, so you need server-side p95 likely under ~70ms to meet the end-to-end goal. That's tight but achievable for smaller models and constrained sequence lengths. We should talk about model choice and quantization.
[00:01:52] Raj: We're evaluating a couple of open models and smaller tuned variants; we also have an on-prem finetuned model but that's more an option if Hosted can't meet latency.
[00:02:00] Liam: Understood. For 64-token responses, sequence length is small so the runtime overhead is mostly attention kernel latency and scheduler overhead. With hosted low-latency runtime we often see p95s in the 40-80ms range for optimized models on our lowest-latency profiles; dedicated pools can be lower and more predictable.
[00:02:18] Sofia: When you say "lowest-latency profiles" what does that map to in hardware? GPUs, CPU inference?
[00:02:24] Liam: Typically A100 or H100 in our Dedicated, and in Hosted we use a mixture — fastest configs may be H100-backed. We also have optimized kernel paths and quantized variants to reduce latency. For extreme low p95 we recommend dedicated with pinned capacity.
[00:02:38] Tom: We prefer not to go straight to Dedicated unless we absolutely need it — cost is a factor. Can Hosted reliably keep p95 under 100ms at 300 concurrency?
[00:02:47] Maya: Good question. It depends on batching and concurrency behavior. Hosted scales horizontally with autoscaling but there is a trade-off: to keep p95 low with high concurrency we can configure routing to favor low-latency nodes and enable pre-warmed capacity. There are also our caching and KV techniques for repeated prefixes which may reduce work.
[00:03:03] Raj: Can you talk about tokens/sec benchmarking? We want to know practical throughput for our sample workload: mix of 64-token and 256-token responses.
[00:03:11] Liam: Sure. For throughput benchmarks we measure tokens/sec at steady-state with realistic concurrency and streaming enabled vs disabled. Example numbers: a single H100 instance with continuous batching might do X tokens/sec for 256-token prompts — (note: some numbers may be approximated here during call). We'll run an exact test against your workload.
[00:03:30] Sofia: We also need accuracy/regression checks — we can't degrade model quality. How do you handle quantization/regression monitoring?
[00:03:37] Liam: We have Redwood Optimize which recommends quantization profiles and runs eval sets. For production we set up regression alerts tied to prompt sets and will trigger rollback or fallback to a non-quantized variant.
[00:03:48] Raj: Security — SOC2, SSO, KMS. We need encryption and audit logs, and for some customers we must have VPC options.
[00:03:56] Maya: We support SOC2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and customer-managed KMS in both Dedicated and Private deployments. Hosted has customer isolation and audit logs; Dedicated adds SLA-backed uptime and private pools; Private gives you a customer-managed control plane in your VPC.
[00:04:10] Tom: For VPC peering, our infra team needs to know egress/IPs and whether mutual TLS is supported.
[00:04:16] Liam: We'll share a VPC deployment checklist and the network contact info. We support TLS and mTLS options, and our control plane can be set up behind customer IR.
[00:04:27] Sofia: Back to latency. What's the impact of streaming on p95? Our front-end uses streaming heavily.
[00:04:33] Liam: Streaming adds a small constant overhead for protocol and chunking but it often improves perceived latency because the user sees tokens earlier. For p95 token-to-first-token you'll usually see lower numbers; full completion p95 might be slightly higher but still within bounds depending on chunk size.
[00:04:49] Raj: So for short responses streaming is probably net positive.
[00:04:52] Liam: Agreed.
[00:04:55] [00:05:00] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[00:05:04] Maya: We'll need your sample traces — can you share a couple of production traces and a small synthetic workload?
[00:05:10] Sofia: Yes, I'll send over a dataset of typical prompts (about 50 samples) and 24-hour trace summaries.
[00:05:16] Raj: Also curious about cold start behavior when instances scale up for bursts.
[00:05:20] Liam: Cold starts depend on the model size and whether it's pre-warmed; we have options for pre-warming and pinned capacity in Dedicated. In Hosted we do warm pools and fast orchestration, but there can be a short warm-up tail — we recommend burst configs or reserved capacity for tight SLAs.
[00:05:36] Tom: Does Redwood expose per-route configs for latency vs cost trade-offs? Like some endpoints go to low-latency pool and others to cheaper high-throughput pool.
[00:05:44] Maya: Yes, Route policies let you map endpoints to policies — latency-first, cost-first, fallback models, region routing, etc.
[00:05:52] Sofia: For benchmarks, can you run token/sec with streaming on? Our traffic will be streaming-heavy.
[00:05:58] Liam: Absolutely — we'll run both streaming and non-streaming tests. Please send us the prompt mix and concurrency profile and we'll mirror it.
[00:06:06] Raj: What's the expected TTL for KV cache and how much of our rate can caching remove?
[00:06:12] Liam: Cache hits depend on repetition in prompts; prefix caching and per-customer KV caches can substantially reduce compute for repeated prefixes — in some workflows we've seen 20-40% token savings. TTL is configurable.
[00:06:24] [00:06:30] Maya: Pricing conversation later — quick note that Dedicated has reserved capacity commitments but predictable per-token and per-hour compute pricing; Hosted is usage-based.
[00:06:40] Raj: One more on metrics: we want p95 measured both server-side (generation time) and end-to-end; can Redwood provide both?
[00:06:47] Liam: Yes, our traces break down token gen time, network, and SDK latency, and we can instrument front-end for end-to-end.
[00:06:55] Sofia: For the benchmark config, we currently use 256-token max, typical prompts are 150 tokens, responses average 80 tokens.
[00:07:04] Liam: Good. We'll run a scenario with prompt 150 + response 80, concurrency 300 steady state, bursts to 500. We'll measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[00:07:13] Tom: Will you be able to share raw logs from the test? We need them for our inbound infra validation.
[00:07:18] Liam: Yes, we'll share anonymized logs and perf traces.
[00:07:22] Raj: A few risky bits: our compliance team insists on customer-managed KMS for secrets. Hosted supports envelope encryption?
[00:07:29] Maya: Hosted supports customer-managed keys for data-at-rest via KMS integration; Dedicated/Private give you more control. We'll include architecture details in the pack we send.
[00:07:39] [00:07:45] Speaker 2: (background)
[00:07:47] Sofia: On fallback strategies — if a quantized variant has a regression what's the automatic behavior?
[00:07:52] Liam: Our rollout supports canary and automatic fallback to previous variant if regression metrics breach thresholds; we also keep non-quantized variants available for immediate failover.
[00:08:02] Raj: What's the SLA on latency for Dedicated? Do you commit to p95 numbers?
[00:08:08] Maya: We typically commit to uptime and latency SLOs at the route level for Dedicated with contractual terms — exact p95 targets can be negotiated based on committed capacity.
[00:08:18] Tom: For the pilot, we want to see a run that simulates our traffic during a 1-hour peak. Can we get a pilot with reserved nodes?
[00:08:25] Liam: We can provision a short-term Dedicated pool or a hosted pre-warmed reserved tier for pilot. We'll size it based on benchmark results.
[00:08:33] Sofia: What about model variant fallback like smaller model when high load? We want graceful degradation not hard errors.
[00:08:40] Liam: Smart routing supports model variant fallback by policy, and you can set cost/latency thresholds per route. That way under heavy load it can route to a cheaper lower-latency variant.
[00:08:50] Raj: That sounds useful.
[00:08:52] [00:09:00] Maya: Quick admin — can I confirm decision timeline? When do you expect to pick a pilot vendor?
[00:09:06] Raj: We're looking to pick by end of September; pilot in early October ideally.
[00:09:11] Maya: Great — we'll align.
[00:09:14] Sofia: Minor nit — our infra team will need the exact IP ranges and egress documentation for peering.
[00:09:20] Tom: And a contact at Redwood for peering setup.
[00:09:23] Liam: I'll be the contact and I'll include network ops details in the checklist.
[00:09:28] [00:09:30] Speaker 3: (typing noises)
[00:09:32] Raj: For tokens/sec numbers do you have a public spreadsheet or benchmark reference?
[00:09:37] Liam: We have internal reference sheets; we'll run the workload and publish the CSV with tokens/sec, latency distribution, and cost estimate.
[00:09:46] Sofia: On cost, can you give a rough delta between Hosted and Dedicated for our expected usage?
[00:09:52] Maya: Ballpark: Dedicated with reserved commit often lowers per-token cost by 20-40% depending on utilization. Hosted gives lower operational overhead but can be more expensive at scale. We'll provide a model with your traffic numbers.
[00:10:05] Tom: Any network considerations for streaming — long-lived connections, websockets?
[00:10:10] Liam: We support streaming via chunked HTTP and websockets. For many clients chunked HTTP is sufficient; websockets are recommended for very high concurrency streaming. We'll test both if you want.
[00:10:22] Raj: Okay, let's talk benchmarks specifics — run with 300 concurrency, prompt 150 tokens, response 80 tokens, streaming on, measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. Also run non-streaming baseline.
[00:10:36] Liam: Got it. We'll run both. Any need to test quantized variants?
[00:10:40] Sofia: Yes run both FP16 and int8 quantized if possible. We need to see quality delta.
[00:10:46] Liam: We'll include both and run eval prompts to assess regressions.
[00:10:50] [00:11:00] Maya: Sounds like a plan. Any blockers for us to start the benchmark?
[00:11:04] Sofia: I'll drop the sample prompts and traces by EOD tomorrow.
[00:11:08] Tom: I'll validate VPC constraints and share the egress list.
[00:11:11] Raj: We'll need NDAs signed before sharing some of the traces.
[00:11:15] Maya: Noted — I'll send the NDA and pricing after the call.
[00:11:19] [00:11:30] Speaker 4: (crosstalk)
[00:11:33] Liam: Quick technical note on concurrency measurement: are you measuring concurrent open connections or concurrent in-flight model calls?
[00:11:40] Raj: In-flight model calls — calls that require GPU work.
[00:11:44] Liam: Ok that matters because connection multiplexing can cause more open sockets but less GPU load. We'll mirror your in-flight metric.
[00:11:51] Sofia: Also our UI opens connections per user session; sometimes fam — sorry — sometimes front-end multiplexes several calls. We'll indicate that in the trace.
[00:11:59] Liam: Great.
[00:12:02] Raj: For the pilot duration, we prefer a week-long run with traffic replay if possible.
[00:12:08] Liam: Week-long pilot is doable; for hosted we'll need to discuss quotas. For dedicated short-term we can provision a week. We'll size nodes accordingly.
[00:12:17] Tom: Does Redwood provide a cost estimate for the pilot upfront?
[00:12:20] Maya: Yes we'll provide a pilot cost estimate with node hours and the expected per-token estimate.
[00:12:24] [00:12:30] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[00:12:32] Sofia: On observability, we need per-route token-level metrics and per-token cost.
[00:12:37] Liam: Console exposes token-level breakdown, latency histograms, and route dashboards. We can also integrate with your telemetry stack.
[00:12:45] Raj: Integration with Datadog would be good.
[00:12:48] Liam: We have Datadog exporters and logs hooks.
[00:12:51] [00:13:00] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps before we run out of time.
[00:13:03] Maya: Action items: Maya to send pricing and NDA; Liam to run throughput benchmarks once Sofia shares sample workload; Sofia to share traces; Tom to share network egress and peering contact.
[00:13:15] Raj: That matches our notes.
[00:13:18] Sofia: One more question: do you have reference customers in payments?
[00:13:22] Maya: Yes we do, we'll share a redacted case study.
[00:13:26] [00:13:30] Tom: Anything else?
[00:13:32] Raj: No, thank you.
[00:13:35] Maya: Great, we'll follow up with the pack. Thanks everyone.
[00:13:40] [01:02:00] (call ends)
